description_full: Marriott International, Inc. engages in the operation, franchising, and licensing of hotel, residential, timeshare, and other lodging properties in the United States, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Greater China, the Asia-Pacific, and internationally. The company operates properties under the JW Marriott, The Ritz-Carlton, The Luxury Collection, W Hotels, St. Regis, EDITION, Bvlgari, Marriott Hotels, Sheraton, Westin, Autograph Collection, Renaissance Hotels, Le Méridien, Delta Hotels by Marriott, MGM Collection with Marriott Bonvoy, Tribute Portfolio, Gaylord Hotels, Design Hotels, Marriott Executive Apartments, Apartments by Marriott Bonvoy, Courtyard by Marriott, Fairfield by Marriott, Residence Inn by Marriott, SpringHill Suites by Marriott, Four Points by Sheraton, TownePlace Suites by Marriott, Aloft Hotels, AC Hotels by Marriott, Moxy Hotels, Element Hotels, Protea Hotels by Marriott, citizenM, City Express by Marriott, and Four Points Flex by Sheraton brands. It also operates residences, timeshares, and yachts. The company was formerly known as New Marriott MI, Inc. and changed its name to Marriott International, Inc. in May 1998. Marriott International, Inc. was founded in 1927 and is headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland.
ceo_bio: Mr. Anthony G. Capuano Jr. | President, CEO & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $6.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 414K people. Revenue per employee of $63K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $6K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $570 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 108× revenue per employee (high relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Marriott International is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $107.2B market cap on $26.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 28% against a 9% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $2.6B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.23× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.1×.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 8pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 1.0% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+88.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.27 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $503.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $215 (margin of safety -94%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $154 to $300 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 41.5 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 25.2 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 41.1 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 56% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 26 covering analysts target $408 on average, 2% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 28% clears the cost of capital of 9.0% by 19pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.11).
It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.23x.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($358.0M of cash against $15.0B of debt), with interest covered 5.1x.
The current ratio of 0.43 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.0% over 3 years, 19.9% over 5 years and 6.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 7.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs 4.2x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 29, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 18.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 64%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (16 sales, net $33.5M sold).
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (3.0% in buybacks and 0.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 414,000 employees, each generates about $63K of revenue, 0.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 5.6% a year.
That works out to $6K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.8M (108x revenue per employee).
